pos: n. pl. (a family of the tribe of Manasseh, descended from Jeezer son of Gilead; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'I'ezri, the family of Jeezer, whose name probably means help, or my help; named once in Scripture, at Numbers 26:30.
biblical_def: The Jeezerites are a clan of Manasseh, named once, in the second numbering of Israel in the plains of Moab: “These are the sons of Gilead: of Jeezer, the family of the Jeezerites: of Helek, the family of the Helekites” (Numbers 26:30). The line is traced in the verse before: “Of the sons of Manasseh: of Machir, the family of the Machirites: and Machir begat Gilead: of Gilead come the family of the Gileadites” (Numbers 26:29). Jeezer's name probably means help, and the clan that bore it is otherwise unrecorded. This census is the one taken after the wilderness generation had died, and that is the whole doctrinal weight of the chapter: God had sworn that the men who refused Canaan would not see it, and the roll of Numbers 26 is the roll of their sons. The same chapter preserves the case that would later establish the daughters' right of inheritance: “And Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters: and the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, and Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah” (Numbers 26:33). And the tribe is totalled: “These are the families of Manasseh, and those that were numbered of them, fifty and two thousand and seven hundred” (Numbers 26:34). A family named once is a family God counted.

corruption_summary: The census chapters are read as administrative residue, when Numbers 26 is the roll of a generation that replaced one God had sworn would not enter the land.
corruption_paragraphs: Numbers 26 is skipped more consistently than almost any chapter in the Pentateuch, and it is one of the most sobering. Every clan in it, the Jeezerites included, exists because the fathers had been excluded by a divine oath. The chapter is the arithmetic of judgment and mercy together: judgment on the men who would not go up, mercy to the sons who did.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God counts families by name, and that a generation may inherit what its fathers forfeited without any of the counting being accidental.

pos: n. pl. (a family of the tribe of Manasseh, descended from Helek son of Gilead; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Chelqi, the family of Helek, whose name means a portion or a share, from chalaq, to divide or apportion; named once in Scripture, at Numbers 26:30.
biblical_def: The Helekites are a clan of Manasseh, named once, in the wilderness census taken in the plains of Moab: “These are the sons of Gilead: of Jeezer, the family of the Jeezerites: of Helek, the family of the Helekites” (Numbers 26:30). The name of their father means a portion or a share, from the verb to divide, and it is the very word used of the apportioning of the land. A clan called Portion is counted in the chapter immediately before the land is portioned out. Their descent runs through Gilead and Machir: “Of the sons of Manasseh: of Machir, the family of the Machirites: and Machir begat Gilead: of Gilead come the family of the Gileadites” (Numbers 26:29). Beside them in the same register stands the family of Hepher, whose son left only daughters: “And Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters” (Numbers 26:33) — the case that would be brought to Moses and would settle the law of a daughter's inheritance. The chapter closes the tribe's account with a number: fifty and two thousand and seven hundred (Numbers 26:34). The portion was real, the men who received it were named, and God kept the ledger.

corruption_summary: Inheritance is treated as a human arrangement, though the very name of this clan is the Hebrew word for the portion God apportions.
corruption_paragraphs: Helek is portion, and the root is the one Scripture uses when God divides the land among the tribes. A clan bearing that name sits in the register taken just before the apportioning, which is the kind of quiet fitness the Holy Ghost works into His records. Inheritance in Scripture is never what men seize; it is what God divides, and the division is by name and by family.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the believer's portion is assigned and not negotiated, and that the God who apportioned Canaan by families apportions the inheritance of the saints the same way.

pos: n. pl. (a family of the tribe of Manasseh, descended from Shemida; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Shemida'i, the family of Shemida, whose name probably means the name of knowing, or fame of knowledge; named once in Scripture, at Numbers 26:32.
biblical_def: The Shemidaites are a clan of Manasseh, named once: “And of Shemida, the family of the Shemidaites: and of Hepher, the family of the Hepherites” (Numbers 26:32). Their father's name is generally read as compounding the Hebrew for a name with a root meaning to know, so that it carries the sense of renown or of knowledge made known. Nothing else is recorded of the family. They belong to the line of Gilead and Machir: “Of the sons of Manasseh: of Machir, the family of the Machirites: and Machir begat Gilead: of Gilead come the family of the Gileadites” (Numbers 26:29). The verse immediately following theirs is one of the most consequential in the chapter: “And Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters: and the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, and Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah” (Numbers 26:33). Those five women would come before Moses and the LORD would grant their petition, and the law of inheritance in Israel was settled by it. The Shemidaites are a name in the margin of a chapter where God was quietly arranging both a conquest and a statute. “These are the families of Manasseh” (Numbers 26:34).

corruption_summary: Scripture's provision for women without brothers is either ignored or pressed into an argument against the order God established elsewhere.
corruption_paragraphs: Zelophehad's daughters stand in the same breath as the Shemidaites, and their case is handled in Scripture with neither indifference nor revolution: the LORD granted their petition and gave them their father's inheritance, while the creational order of headship in home and church stands untouched throughout the same law. Both are God's word. A reading that must choose between them has imported a conflict Scripture does not have.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God provides particular justice for particular cases without amending His general order, and that He hears petitions brought by those with no one else to speak for them.

pos: n. pl. (a family of the tribe of Manasseh, descended from Hepher, the father of Zelophehad; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Chephri, the family of Hepher, whose name means a pit or a well, from chaphar, to dig; named once in Scripture, at Numbers 26:32.
biblical_def: The Hepherites are a clan of Manasseh, named once: “And of Shemida, the family of the Shemidaites: and of Hepher, the family of the Hepherites” (Numbers 26:32). The name of their father means a pit or a well, from the verb to dig. They are the most consequential of the obscure clans in this chapter, because of the very next verse: “And Zelophehad the son of Hepher had no sons, but daughters: and the names of the daughters of Zelophehad were Mahlah, and Noah, Hoglah, Milcah, and Tirzah” (Numbers 26:33). Zelophehad was a Hepherite, and the five sisters brought their father's case to Moses at the door of the tabernacle; the LORD's answer gave them the inheritance and established the statute for every like case in Israel. So a clan named for a dug well becomes the occasion of a law. The family's descent runs the same course as the rest: “Machir begat Gilead: of Gilead come the family of the Gileadites” (Numbers 26:29), and the tribal total is given at the end: “These are the families of Manasseh, and those that were numbered of them, fifty and two thousand and seven hundred” (Numbers 26:34).

corruption_summary: The statutes of the Pentateuch are dismissed as arbitrary, when Numbers shows a law arising from a real family's real case brought before the LORD.
corruption_paragraphs: The law of a daughter's inheritance did not descend as an abstraction; it came because five Hepherite women stood at the tabernacle door and asked. Moses brought their cause before the LORD and the LORD answered. That is how a great deal of the Pentateuch's case law reads, and it answers the charge that these statutes are the arbitrary leavings of a priestly caste: they have families and names attached.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the LORD gives law in answer to real need, and that a clan named for a well in the ground became the occasion of a statute for all Israel.

pos: n. pl. (an ancient people of the southern desert, raided by David from Ziklag; named once)
etymology: Hebrew Gizri, of uncertain reference; the Authorized Version margin at 1 Samuel 27:8 offers the alternative reading “Gerzites.” Named once in Scripture.
biblical_def: The Gezrites are named once, among the peoples David raided during his exile in Philistine territory: “And David and his men went up, and invaded the Geshurites, and the Gezrites, and the Amalekites: for those nations were of old the inhabitants of the land, as thou goest to Shur, even unto the land of Egypt” (1 Samuel 27:8). The Authorized Version notes a variant reading in the margin, Gerzites, and nothing further is known of them beyond that they were an old desert people on the Egyptian road. The passage is not a flattering one for David. He was living under Achish of Gath, and he covered his raids with a lie: “And Achish said, Whither have ye made a road to day? And David said, Against the south of Judah, and against the south of the Jerahmeelites, and against the south of the Kenites” (1 Samuel 27:10). To keep the deception airtight he left no witnesses: “And David smote the land, and left neither man nor woman alive” (1 Samuel 27:9). And it worked: “And Achish believed David, saying, He hath made his people Israel utterly to abhor him; therefore he shall be my servant for ever” (1 Samuel 27:12). Scripture records the man after God's own heart deceiving a heathen king, and does not pause to excuse it.

corruption_summary: The sins of biblical heroes are explained away, where Scripture reports David's deception of Achish plainly and leaves the reader to judge it by the law.
corruption_paragraphs: The common handling of 1 Samuel 27 is to justify David on grounds of necessity, or to treat the chapter as morally neutral reporting. Neither is required. Scripture records the lie and the killing that covered it without comment, exactly as it records Abraham in Egypt and Peter in the hall. The inspired writers do not protect their subjects. That honesty is one of the strongest internal evidences that these books are not propaganda, and it leaves the law of God as the standard by which the hero is measured.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the man after God's own heart needed a Saviour as much as the Gezrites did, and that Scripture's refusal to flatter him is a mercy to every reader who sins.

pos: n. pl. (the idolatrous priests of Baal in Judah, marked for destruction; named once)
etymology: Hebrew kemarim, idol-priests, from a root meaning to be black or to be scorched, probably from their black vestments or from the burnt offerings they tended; named once in Scripture, at Zephaniah 1:4.
biblical_def: The Chemarims are the idolatrous priesthood of Judah, named once, in the sentence God passed on Jerusalem through Zephaniah: “I will also stretch out mine hand upon Judah, and upon all the inhabitants of Jerusalem; and I will cut off the remnant of Baal from this place, and the name of the Chemarims with the priests” (Zephaniah 1:4). The Hebrew word is used elsewhere only of the priests of the high places, and it probably comes from a root meaning to be black, whether from their vestments or from the smoke of what they burned. Note what the verse promises to cut off: not the men only but the name, which is to say the office itself is to be abolished. And note who stands beside them: the verse sets the Chemarims with the priests, that is, the legitimate Aaronic order, condemned in the same clause for tolerating what they should have torn down. The next verses describe the religion actually being practised: “And them that worship the host of heaven upon the housetops; and them that worship and that swear by the LORD, and that swear by Malcham” (Zephaniah 1:5), and then “them that are turned back from the LORD; and those that have not sought the LORD, nor enquired for him” (Zephaniah 1:6). Swearing by the LORD and by Malcham together is the sin; God will not share an altar.

corruption_summary: Syncretism is presented as generous inclusion, when Zephaniah 1:5 names swearing by the LORD and by Malcham together as the thing for which a priesthood is abolished.
corruption_paragraphs: The men Zephaniah condemns were not atheists. They swore by the LORD — and also by Malcham. That is the exact structure of every syncretism since: the true God retained in the list, with others added beside Him, and the arrangement defended as breadth. God's answer is to cut off the name of the priesthood that administered it, and to condemn in the same clause the lawful priests who permitted it. Inclusion that adds to the first commandment is not generosity; it is the sin for which Judah lost her temple.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God will not be worshipped alongside another, and that officers who tolerate false worship share the sentence of those who conduct it.

pos: n. pl. (the inhabitants of Gaza, who laid wait for Samson in the gate; named once)
etymology: Hebrew 'Azzathi, an inhabitant of Gaza, from 'Azzah, Gaza, the strong place; named once in Scripture, at Judges 16:2.
biblical_def: The Gazites are the men of Gaza, named once, lying in ambush for Samson: “And it was told the Gazites, saying, Samson is come hither. And they compassed him in, and laid wait for him all night in the gate of the city, and were quiet all the night, saying, In the morning, when it is day, we shall kill him” (Judges 16:2). Samson had come to Gaza on no business of God's, and the ambush was shrewd: a walled city has one way out, and they held it. He rose at midnight and carried the gates away, posts and bar and all. The Gazites lost that round, but the chapter is not a story of a man winning. It is the story of a Nazarite spending his strength on his appetites until the strength was taken, and the city he had humiliated got him in the end: “But the Philistines took him, and put out his eyes, and brought him down to Gaza, and bound him with fetters of brass; and he did grind in the prison house” (Judges 16:21). He came back to Gaza blind, and in Gaza he died, and the Holy Ghost records the arithmetic of it without sentiment: “So the dead which he slew at his death were more than they which he slew in his life” (Judges 16:30).

corruption_summary: Samson is read as a folk hero of strength, when Judges presents him as a man whose gift outlasted his self-government until God took it from him.
corruption_paragraphs: The popular Samson is a strongman; the Samson of Judges 16 is a Nazarite who went to Gaza for a harlot and ended grinding in a Philistine mill with his eyes put out. The chapter is not about muscle but about a consecrated man who treated his consecration as a possession. God gave him one more act of strength at the end, in answer to prayer, and the text is careful to say he killed more in dying than in living — which is a verdict on the living.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that gifts are held in trust and may be withdrawn, and that a man may carry away the gates of a city and still be a slave to what is inside himself.

pos: n. (a Hebrew woman; used once, of the bondwomen Zedekiah's covenant was to set free)
etymology: English feminine of Hebrew, formed with the suffix -ess, rendering the Hebrew feminine 'Ibriyyah; used once in Scripture, at Jeremiah 34:9.
biblical_def: Hebrewess is the Authorized Version's feminine of Hebrew, and it occurs once, in the terms of a covenant Zedekiah made and broke: “That every man should let his manservant, and every man his maidservant, being an Hebrew or an Hebrewess, go free; that none should serve himself of them, to wit, of a Jew his brother” (Jeremiah 34:9). The word exists in the English text because the law being invoked covered women as explicitly as men — the Mosaic statute of release did not stop at the manservant. The occasion was a late and frightened reformation: “This is the word that came unto Jeremiah from the LORD, after that the king Zedekiah had made a covenant with all the people which were at Jerusalem, to proclaim liberty unto them” (Jeremiah 34:8). Then the siege lifted for a season, and they took their slaves back: “But afterward they turned, and caused the servants and the handmaids, whom they had let go free, to return, and brought them into subjection for servants and for handmaids” (Jeremiah 34:11). The LORD's answer is one of the most terrible sentences in the prophets: “behold, I proclaim a liberty for you, saith the LORD, to the sword, to the pestilence, and to the famine” (Jeremiah 34:17). They would have a liberty, since they loved the word so much.

corruption_summary: Repentance under pressure is mistaken for repentance, when Jeremiah 34 shows a reform made in a siege and reversed the moment the siege lifted.
corruption_paragraphs: Zedekiah's release was genuine on paper and lasted exactly as long as the danger. That is the test Jeremiah 34 applies to every crisis conversion: not what a man promises while the army is at the wall, but what he does when it withdraws. The sentence is fitted to the crime with terrible precision — they would not proclaim liberty, so God proclaimed one, to the sword and the pestilence and the famine.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's law reached the maidservant as directly as the manservant, and that a covenant made before God and then reversed is worse than one never made.

pos: n. pl. (one of the transplanted peoples of Samaria who wrote against the rebuilding of the temple; named once)
etymology: Aramaic Dinaye, of uncertain reference, perhaps a people of Media or of the region about Dinah; named once in Scripture, at Ezra 4:9.
biblical_def: The Dinaites are named once, at the head of a list of transplanted peoples who joined in the letter sent to Artaxerxes against the rebuilding of the temple: “Then wrote Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions; the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites” (Ezra 4:9). They were among the nations the Assyrian kings had settled in Samaria, and nothing else is recorded of them. The chapter explains who such people were to the returned captives: “Now when the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin heard that the children of the captivity builded the temple unto the LORD God of Israel” (Ezra 4:1). Their method was not the sword but discouragement and paperwork: “Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building” (Ezra 4:4). And for a time it worked, which is the sober note the chapter ends on: “Then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem. So it ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia” (Ezra 4:24). A letter stopped what an army had not.

corruption_summary: Opposition to the work of God is expected to come as persecution, when Ezra 4 shows it coming as discouragement and correspondence.
corruption_paragraphs: No one in Ezra 4 drew a sword. The adversaries of Judah weakened hands, raised troubles, and wrote a letter — and the house of God stood unfinished for years. That is the ordinary shape of opposition to real work: not martyrdom but attrition, delay, process, and the steady erosion of nerve. A people who are braced for persecution and unprepared for discouragement will be stopped by the lesser weapon.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that the work resumed when prophets were sent to the builders, and that the answer to weakened hands is the preaching of the word rather than a better letter.

pos: n. pl. (one of the transplanted peoples of Samaria named in the letter against the temple; named once)
etymology: Aramaic Apharsaye, of uncertain reference, by some taken for Persians; named once in Scripture, at Ezra 4:9.
biblical_def: The Apharsites are named once, in the same roll of peoples who signed against the temple: “Then wrote Rehum the chancellor, and Shimshai the scribe, and the rest of their companions; the Dinaites, the Apharsathchites, the Tarpelites, the Apharsites, the Archevites, the Babylonians, the Susanchites, the Dehavites, and the Elamites” (Ezra 4:9). Some have taken the name for Persians; the honest answer is that it is of uncertain reference, like most of that list. What the list is for is plain enough. Nine peoples, resettled in Samaria by conquerors, are gathered behind a chancellor and a scribe to oppose a building project, and the opposition is framed as loyalty to the throne. The chapter has already told the reader what to call them: “the adversaries of Judah and Benjamin” (Ezra 4:1). Their first instrument was pressure — “Then the people of the land weakened the hands of the people of Judah, and troubled them in building” (Ezra 4:4) — and their second was the royal post. The result is recorded without comfort: “Then ceased the work of the house of God which is at Jerusalem. So it ceased unto the second year of the reign of Darius king of Persia” (Ezra 4:24). God's house waited on a king's calendar, and God was not thereby defeated.

corruption_summary: Hostility to the church is given a respectable civic dress, as it was in Ezra 4, where opposition to the temple was presented to the throne as loyal concern.
corruption_paragraphs: The letter in Ezra 4 does not say that the builders worship the wrong God. It says they are a rebellious city and a danger to royal revenue. Opposition to God's work almost always arrives in that costume — public order, good governance, the common interest — and it is far more effective in that dress than in open blasphemy. Ezra names the signatories anyway, and calls them adversaries.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is that God's house was delayed and not defeated, and that the pause between Cyrus and Darius was as much under His hand as the decree that ended it.
